Constitutional Framework: Governed under Part X (Article 244(1)) and the Fifth Schedule for the administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.
Declaring Authority: The President of India declares and notifies an area as a Scheduled Area

Scope of State Executive Power: Declaration of a Scheduled Area does NOT make it a Union Territory, create a separate state, or terminate the State Government's executive power—State executive power continues to extend over Scheduled Areas subject to the Fifth Schedule.

Tribal Advisory Council (TAC): Mandatory advisory body established in each State having Scheduled Areas (under Paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule) to advise on matters pertaining to the welfare and advancement of Scheduled Tribes.

Governor's Annual Report: The Governor submits a report regarding the administration of Scheduled Areas directly to the President of India (annually or whenever required by the President); Trap: It is submitted by the Governor to the President, NOT by the Chief Minister to the Union Home Ministry.
Protection of Tribal Land (Paragraph 5): The Governor is empowered to make regulations prohibiting or restricting the transfer of tribal land to non-tribals and regulating money-lending to STs.

Samatha v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1997) Landmark Ruling: The Supreme Court held that the transfer/lease of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private parties for mining operations is null, void, and inoperative under the Fifth Schedule.

Definition: The inherent constitutional power of the higher judiciary to examine the constitutionality of legislative enactments and executive orders, declaring them void if they contravene constitutional provisions.
Exercising Authority: Vested jointly in the Supreme Court (Article 32) and the High Courts (Article 226) (NOT the Supreme Court alone).
Borrowed Source: Adopted from the USA (originated in Marbury v. Madison, 1803 by Chief Justice John Marshall).

Constitutional Supremacy vs. Parliamentary Sovereignty: India: Constitutional Supremacy with Judicial Review; UK: Parliamentary Sovereignty (No traditional judicial review of primary parliamentary legislation).

t: Basic Structure Integration: In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and reaffirmed in Minerva Mills (1980), Judicial Review under Articles 32 and 226 was declared an integral part of the Basic Structure of the Constitution; Parliament cannot abrogate it even via Article 368.
Review of Constitutional Amendments: Constitutional amendments are themselves subject to Judicial Review on the touchstone of the Basic Structure doctrine.
The 9th Schedule Shield (1st CAA, 1951): Added Articles 31A, 31B, and the 9th Schedule to insulate agrarian and land-reform laws from judicial review on Fundamental Rights grounds.
The 9th Schedule Shield (1st CAA, 1951): Enacted largely to overcome early judicial interpretations restricting state welfare/land acquisition measures.
What Judicial Review is NOT: It is NOT the court questioning the political wisdom, policy merits, or advisability of legislation.
What Judicial Review is NOT: It is NOT automatic pre-assent scrutiny of Bills.
What Judicial Review is NOT: It is NOT an ordinary appellate proceeding.

Federal vs. Unitary Classification Trap: Judicial Review reinforces the Federal principle (preserves constitutional distribution of powers and enforces constitutional limits); It is NOT a Unitary element (unlike All India Services, Governor's appointment, or emergency provisions).

Rajya Sabha Domicile / Voter Requirement (2003 Amendment): Prior to 2003, a candidate contesting for Rajya Sabha had to be an elector in that particular State.

Rajya Sabha Domicile / Voter Requirement (2003 Amendment): The 2003 Amendment removed this requirement; any registered elector in India can contest from any State. Upheld by the SC in Kuldip Nayar (2006).

Death of a Contesting Candidate (1996 Amendment): Elections are no longer countermanded automatically upon the death of a candidate; recognized political parties are permitted to nominate a replacement within a set timeframe.

National Party Criteria: A political party must win at least 6% of the total valid votes in four or more states during a Lok Sabha (Lok Sabha general election) or State Legislative Assembly election, AND it must also win at least 4 Lok Sabha seats from any state or states.
National Party Criteria: Alternatively, a party must win at least 2% of the total seats in the Lok Sabha (which equals 11 seats), and these elected members must come from at least 3 different states.
National Party Criteria: Alternatively, a party must be officially recognized as a State Party in at least 4 different states.
Model Code of Conduct (MCC): Comes into force immediately upon the formal announcement of the election schedule by the ECI.

Merger Protection Exception: Disqualification on grounds of defection does not apply if a party merges with another and ≥ 2/3rd of the members of the legislative party agree to the merger (The original 1/3rd "split" exemption was omitted by the 91st CAA, 2003).
Scope of Disqualification: Applies to members voluntarily giving up party membership or voting/abstaining contrary to party whips without prior permission.
